items.enunciado:
You are going to read a magazine article about unusual hobbies. For questions 31–36, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
Text
Beyond the Mainstream: The Appeal of Unusual Hobbies
In an age when leisure time is often filled with predictable pursuits, a growing number of people are turning to hobbies that friends and colleagues find difficult to classify. What may look eccentric from the outside frequently turns out, for those who practise it, to be a carefully chosen counterbalance to routine work and digital distraction.
One example is competitive jigsaw puzzling, which has developed a serious following in several countries. Enthusiasts gather for timed events where teams race to complete complex images under strict rules. Outsiders sometimes assume the activity is purely relaxing, yet participants describe intense concentration and genuine pride when a difficult design finally fits together. For many, the appeal lies not in winning alone but in sharing a slow, tactile process that contrasts sharply with the instant feedback of screen-based entertainment.
Historical reenactment offers a different kind of escape. Men and women spend weekends recreating battles or domestic life from past centuries, investing considerable money in authentic costumes and equipment. Critics may question whether such devotion to the past is worthwhile, but reenactors argue that handling reproduction tools and learning forgotten skills gives them a vivid sense of how earlier generations lived. Several groups also visit schools, hoping to make history feel immediate rather than abstract.
Then there are pursuits such as letterboxing and geocaching, in which participants follow clues to locate hidden containers in parks, towns or countryside. The hobby blends navigation, puzzle-solving and mild adventure, and it encourages exploration of places that walkers might otherwise ignore. Unlike some outdoor sports, it rarely demands exceptional fitness; instead, patience and curiosity matter more. Many participants say the greatest reward is discovering a quiet corner of their own region that they had never noticed before.
What these activities share is not oddity for its own sake. People often choose them because mainstream options no longer feel stimulating, or because they want a hobby that reflects a particular identity. An office worker who restores vintage radios at night, for instance, may value the feeling of repairing something tangible in a job dominated by emails. Similarly, a teenager who collects and restores mechanical typewriters may enjoy the mechanical rhythm and the surprise of younger friends who have never seen one.
Unusual hobbies can also create communities that cut across age and background. Clubs, festivals and online forums allow beginners to learn from experienced practitioners without facing the pressure of formal competition. The author of a recent survey noted that respondents rarely described their hobbies as attempts to impress others; instead, they emphasised personal challenge, creativity and the pleasure of belonging to a small group that understands a shared obsession.
None of this suggests that conventional pastimes are inferior. Yoga, team sports and cinema remain popular for good reason. Yet the spread of less familiar hobbies reminds us that leisure is deeply personal. What seems baffling at first glance may simply be someone's deliberate search for meaning, focus and connection in an otherwise hurried world.

Questions
31. What does the writer suggest about many competitive jigsaw enthusiasts? A. They value a slow, hands-on activity that differs from instant digital entertainment. B. They take part mainly because timed events offer guaranteed prizes. C. They prefer working alone rather than sharing the experience with others. D. They treat the hobby as a simple way to relax after demanding work.
32. How does the writer present historical reenactment? A. As a hobby that professional historians now recommend without reservation. B. As an activity that has become less appealing to younger participants. C. As a pursuit that depends mainly on expensive equipment rather than skill. D. As something critics doubt, although participants believe it has real value.
33. According to the text, what makes letterboxing and geocaching distinctive? A. They require a level of fitness comparable to serious mountaineering. B. They reward patience and curiosity more than exceptional physical strength. C. They have declined in popularity since navigation technology became widespread. D. They are designed chiefly for people who already know an area extremely well.
34. The examples of vintage radio restoration and typewriter collecting imply that unusual hobbies can A. remove the need for any challenging aspects of paid employment. B. help people recover quickly from long periods of professional stress. C. provide a tangible contrast to work that feels largely intangible. D. be understood immediately by colleagues without any explanation.
35. What did the recent survey suggest about people's reasons for choosing unusual hobbies? A. They wanted mainly to impress people outside their hobby group. B. They valued personal challenge and belonging to a shared-interest community. C. They hoped their hobbies would soon become conventional mainstream activities. D. They were chiefly motivated by the prospect of turning the hobby into a career.
36. Which statement best reflects the writer's overall attitude? A. Mainstream leisure activities are less worthwhile than unusual hobbies. B. People who choose unusual hobbies are largely rejecting modern society. C. Seemingly strange hobbies may reflect a deliberate search for focus and connection. D. Unusual hobbies are likely to disappear as conventional entertainment improves.

You are going to read an article about the rise of community projects in modern towns. Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose from the sentences A–G the one which fits each gap. There is one extra sentence which you do not need to use.
Text
Beyond the Council: Community Projects in Modern Towns
For decades, local problems in towns were often left to municipal authorities alone. Residents might complain at public meetings, yet few expected to play an active role in finding solutions. That attitude has shifted noticeably in recent years. Across many countries, ordinary citizens have begun organising community projects that address issues ranging from neglected green spaces to social isolation among elderly neighbours. (31) ______
These initiatives rarely replace professional services entirely. Instead, they fill gaps that overstretched councils cannot always cover. A volunteer-run repair café, for example, does not put qualified electricians out of work, but it does keep usable appliances out of landfill and teaches practical skills that schools seldom have time to offer. (32) ______ Such events also create informal meeting places where people who might never cross paths otherwise can exchange advice, tools and local news.
One reason these projects have multiplied is that digital tools have lowered the cost of coordination. A single online message can summon twenty helpers for a weekend litter pick or a pop-up food bank, and photographs of the results can attract further support within hours. (33) ______ However, organisers quickly discover that enthusiasm alone does not sustain long-term work; without clear roles and regular communication, even promising groups fade away within months.
Success often depends on partnerships. Schools, charities and small businesses frequently lend space, equipment or expertise when residents propose a plausible plan. In one coastal town, a closed shopfront became a weekly advice hub after the owner offered it rent-free for twelve months. (34) ______ This shared investment makes participants feel that the project belongs to the whole neighbourhood, not to one determined individual who may eventually move away.
Not every attempt thrives. Some groups struggle with funding, while others disagree about priorities or burn out after an initial burst of energy. (35) ______ Yet where projects endure, they tend to reshape how residents view their town: streets once seen as anonymous become familiar, and complaints about what "someone else" should do gradually give way to discussions about what "we" could try next.
The broader impact should not be underestimated. Research in several European cities suggests that areas with active community networks report higher trust between neighbours and a greater willingness to help strangers in minor emergencies. (36) ______ For planners and elected officials, these findings offer a reminder that lasting urban improvement is not solely a matter of infrastructure budgets and zoning regulations.
In the end, the rise of community projects reflects a wider cultural change. People still expect councils to maintain roads and collect refuse, but many no longer wait passively for institutions to solve every local difficulty. They experiment, collaborate and occasionally fail — and in doing so, they redefine what a modern town can feel like from the inside.

Sentences
A For many participants, this marks a shift from simply identifying problems to taking shared responsibility for them.
B This hands-on approach turns abstract environmental concerns into everyday action.
C As a result, ideas that once required months of planning can now be tested within days.
D These contributions may seem modest, yet they allow volunteers to focus on people rather than paperwork.
E Even so, many residents remain convinced that small-scale action is worth the effort.
F Such outcomes suggest that informal networks deserve a place alongside formal policy.
G Yet many young people continue to leave smaller towns in search of better career prospects.

40 was warned by people at work that the change could be risky?
41 appreciates not being tied to one workplace or fixed timetable?
42 prefers a practical, physically active job to working at a desk?
43 uses experience from a previous technical career to explain things clearly?
44 feels rewarded when other people understand difficult ideas?
45 accepts tiring working conditions because the work feels more personally meaningful?
46 combines analytical ability from a previous job with creative work?

Texts
A – Emma Thomson
After a decade working as a marketing executive, Emma decided to follow her passion for literature. She left her corporate job to become a freelance writer, even though several colleagues warned her that she was taking a risk. Though the initial phase was challenging — finding clients and managing irregular income — she found joy in crafting stories and articles on her own terms. Emma appreciates the flexibility that comes with freelancing, allowing her to work from anywhere and set her own schedule. Despite the instability, the creative satisfaction she derives from writing outweighs the financial unpredictability, and she has no intention of returning to office life.
________________________________________
B – Michael Green
Michael was a successful civil engineer before he decided to pursue a career in education. Motivated by a desire to inspire young minds, he retrained as a secondary school teacher during evenings and weekends while still working full time. The transition was not easy, as it required him to adapt to a completely different work environment and daily schedule. However, Michael finds teaching immensely rewarding, particularly when he sees his students grasp complex concepts for the first time. He values the opportunity to impact future generations positively, and he believes his earlier career gave him useful skills in planning and explaining technical ideas clearly.
________________________________________
C – Sophia Martinez
Sophia worked as a software developer for several years before realising that her true calling was in the culinary arts. Leaving a stable job in tech, she enrolled in culinary school to pursue her dream of becoming a chef. Although it was a significant change, Sophia has not looked back since opening her own small restaurant in her home town. She enjoys the hands-on aspect of her new job and the chance to express her creativity through food, despite the long and demanding hours. For her, the physical pace of a kitchen feels more authentic than sitting at a desk, even when service nights are exhausting.
________________________________________
D – Liam Robinson
Liam's journey from accountant to interior designer might seem unusual, but for him it was a natural progression. Always passionate about aesthetics and design, he took the bold step of switching careers after ten years in finance. Liam initially worried about the financial implications of starting again in a competitive field, but he ultimately found a niche for himself, blending his analytical skills with creative design. He appreciates how his new career allows him to see the tangible results of his work, transforming rooms and offices to meet clients' needs. Former colleagues sometimes tease him about the change, yet he feels he is finally doing what suits him best.
________________________________________

items.descripcionParte: Part 17: In this part of the test, you will have a discussion with your partner about the image shown below. You need to discuss the various topics and themes visible in the image, giving your opinions and exchanging ideas. The discussion should last about 4 minutes.
items.enunciado:
In this part of the exam, you will discuss some questions with your partner about the topic of urban life and technology. Try to give detailed answers and support your opinions with examples.
How has technology changed the way people live in cities?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of using smart technology in urban areas?
Do you think public transport in cities will become more efficient with technological advances? Why or why not?
How can technology help to solve environmental problems in cities?
In what ways might urban life become more challenging due to increasing reliance on technology?
Do you prefer living in a city with advanced technology or in a rural area with less technology? Why?
